title: Education Is Hendrick the Heir to Hattie? Selling Elite-Backed Education Models as 'Sciencey' Vainker, Stephen
author: Vainker, Stephen
summary: Education researcher Stephen Vainker presents a critical investigation into Carl Hendrick's professional relationships and potential undisclosed conflicts of interest in his science-of-learning promotion work. Vainker draws a parallel to John Hattie, whose Visible Learning meta-analysis became influential by packaging elite-favored educational models as scientifically backed -- a pattern Vainker argues Hendrick is replicating. The article documents Hendrick's professional connection to Alpha school, a private microschool whose self-directed learning model stands in tension with the direct instruction principles Hendrick typically promotes. Vainker's concern is not only about Hendrick personally but about a broader pattern in which popularizers of educational research earn credibility by presenting findings as more certain and more applicable to commercial products than the research supports. The article raises questions about how conflicts of interest in education research communication should be disclosed and how educators should evaluate credentialing claims from practitioners who simultaneously serve as advocates.
points: Hattie's Visible Learning became the most cited education meta-analysis despite serious methodological critiques, in part because it provided 'effect sizes' vocabulary to justify choices elite schools and ed-reform funders already wanted to make -- a template Vainker argues Hendrick is following.

Hendrick's employment at Alpha school -- whose self-paced, student-directed model contradicts the explicit instruction and retrieval practice research he popularizes -- creates a conflict of interest not disclosed to his 23,000+ Substack readers.

The economic structure of educational thought leadership creates systematic incentives to market research-backed models rather than communicate research honestly: credibility is built on appearing scientific, but revenue comes from schools and publishers.

When a trusted popularizer of learning science promotes research that aligns with a school that employs them, readers cannot assess the promotion without knowing about the employment relationship -- a disclosure norm routine in medicine but absent in education.

Education lacks the disclosure norms of medical research and journalism that would require practitioners to declare conflicts of interest when publishing to mass audiences on the strength of scientific authority.
